title: Feasibility and optimum recovery in warm-start quantum optimization for a drug-response model on a trapped-ion processor
authors: Tanzir Hossain, Rajib Rana, Prabal Datta Barua, Abu Ali Ibn Sina, Niall Higgins, Pascal Elahi, Robert Sang, Bjorn W. Schuller
abstract: On a seven-compound drug-response model, warm-start quantum approximate optimization (QAOA) on IonQ Forte-1 returned valid assignments more often than random bitstrings, but this alone did not show effective optimization. Ideal QAOA raised optimum probability above uniform feasible sampling in only four of twelve reference circuits. Hardware often fell below its own noiseless circuits, while greedy search solved all hardware models within 200 objective evaluations. Expanded simulations showed a gain over feasible sampling in 28 of 35 CAMA-1 panels and none of four 647-V panels. Annealing solved all these panels in every seed. A Grover mixer preserved feasibility and improved optimum probability over feasible sampling in all ten tested models. We analyzed 25 completed tasks containing 5,300 shots from 18 circuits and 14 instances. The encodings use 6-35 qubits and at most 4,900 feasible assignments, which we enumerated to establish exact optima. Noiseless references now cover both the original six circuits and six wider circuits. At 35 qubits, with 4,900 feasible assignments, ideal feasibility was 35.85%, compared with 7 of 200 valid hardware outputs. Its ideal optimum probability was below both sampling controls. The circuits sample assignments in a model built from measured single-agent and pairwise responses.
summary: This work evaluates the performance of warm-start QAOA on a drug-response optimization problem using a trapped-ion quantum processor. The authors compare quantum results against classical heuristics and ideal theoretical bounds, finding that while quantum methods show some promise, classical search algorithms often perform comparably or better on current hardware. The study highlights the significant gap between ideal quantum performance and actual hardware realization.
main_problem: The paper investigates the distinction between improving feasibility and improving optimization when using warm-start Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving constrained optimization problems.
main_result: While warm-start QAOA showed some improvement over random sampling, the authors argue that the performance gains are often marginal compared to classical methods like greedy search or simulated annealing, and hardware performance degrades significantly with increasing qubit count.
method: The study compares quantum circuit outputs (QAOA) against classical baselines, including uniform feasible sampling, greedy local search, and simulated annealing, using a drug-response model.
model_or_system: The problem is formulated using a drug-response model derived from the DREAM dataset, encoded onto a quantum circuit structure simulated on a trapped-ion processor (IonQ Forte-1).
key_observables: Feasibility percentage ($P_F$), probability of achieving the global optimum ($P_\star$), and the number of objective evaluations required by classical search methods.
important_parameters: Qubit count (up to 35), number of compounds, and the structure of the feasible set ($|F|$ up to 4,900).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing hardware measurements (with 95% Wilson intervals) against noiseless ideal simulations and theoretical sampling controls.
figures_summary: Figures compare feasibility and optimum recovery rates across various qubit counts, contrasting hardware results with ideal QAOA and uniform feasible sampling controls.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares warm-start QAOA against multiple classical and theoretical controls (random, feasible sampling, greedy search, annealing) across multiple instances of a drug-response model on a trapped-ion platform.
why_interesting: It provides a detailed, empirical benchmark of near-term quantum optimization algorithms (QAOA) on real hardware for a complex combinatorial problem, directly addressing the gap between theoretical quantum advantage and current hardware limitations.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1. Feasibility with classical and noiseless controls. (A) Original six circuits. (B) Larger circuits, with individual hardware executions offset horizontally and feasible-space sizes below qubit counts. Hardware error bars are pointwise 95% Wilson intervals. Other series are numerically evaluated probabilities; repeated tasks share one ideal circuit reference. Lines guide the eye across different instances and do not imply a scaling law.

Figure 2. Optimum recovery with appropriate controls. (A) Per-shot optimum probability; hardware error bars are pointwise 95% Wilson intervals, including an upper bound when no optimum is observed. Markers are offset slightly for visibility. (B) Calculated probability of at least one optimum in 200 independent samples from the three analytic distributions, using Equation 5. Panel B uses analytic probabilities and assumes independent draws.
